newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Protests delay Sri Lanka coal power plant.
newsitem.headline: Protests delay Sri Lanka coal power plant.

text.p: Outside inteference has prompted civilians in a remote coastal village to turn against plans for Sri Lanka's first coal-fired power plant, Power and Energy Minister Anuruddha Ratwatte said on Friday.

Ratwatte said a feasibility study to set up a 300-megawatt coal power plant at Kalpitiya, in the Puttalam district, 160 km (100 miles) north of the capital Colombo, had come to a halt because of opposition from people.

"But they are not local people. Interested parties have come to the scene from outside," he told a news conference. "It may even be a lobby which does not like coal power to come to our country," he added without elabroating.

State power utility Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) officials said a 300-acre plot of land on the west coast had been surveyed and boundaries demarcated, leaving two villages to its north and south untouched.
Soil testing and other research, which was to be carried out jointly with a team of Swiss consultants, have been delayed after workers were threatened.
In April, one man was killed and several others were injured when police fired at a group of about 5,000 people demonstrating against the planned power plant.
Residents have said they oppose the project because of fears of environmental pollution and loss of land. The

government says most of the 50 fishing and farming families living on the project's perimeter will be unaffected by the plant and that the few families dispalced by the project will be given new land and housing.
"Work is being prevented because of misinformation. In the name of development, we appeal to the people not to yield to false propaganda," Ratwatte said.

CEB chairman Arjun Deraniyagala told the same news conference it was necessary for the plant to begin servicing the national grid as scheduled by 2003, due to the CEB's long-term plans to reduce Sri Lanka's current high dependence on hydropower.

Sri Lanka plans to reduce it reliance on hydropower supply, which currently make up 85 percent of grid power, to 57 percent after a crippling drought last year forced the government to impose daily eight-hour power cuts.
Water levels dropped to dangerous levels again this year with the failure of the northeast monsoon and the delayed onset of intermonsoon showers.

Tropical Sri Lanka has two rainy seasons. The southwest monsoon, the most important for fuelling hydroelectrict plants, which usually starts by June, has also been delayed by about a week, the Meteorology Department said.

Sri Lanka has an installed capacity of 1,115 megawatts of hydropower and 250 megawatts of thermal power, Ratwatte said. The CEB has said it plans to cut dependence on hydropower by building more thermal power plants and buying electricity from private plants.
The first two, a 115-megawatt gas turbine and a 40-megawatt diesel plant, will be on stream before the end of June, Ratwatte said.
